label: Chapter 3: The Gibraltar of the North, 1443 to 1815

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: If the first part of the story was about a dynasty, this part is about a rock.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For the next three and a half centuries, Luxembourg's main job in European politics was to be a fortress.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And it was a good one. A great deal of the time, the Luxembourgers themselves weren't the ones deciding who owned it.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: We left it with Philip the Good of Burgundy in 1443.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And for a while Luxembourg was one piece in a glittering Burgundian empire that included Flanders, Brabant, and Holland.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Burgundy was the richest, most fashionable court in Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But it didn't last. In 1477, Philip's grandson Charles the Bold was killed in battle outside the city of Nancy, leaving a single daughter, Mary.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who married Maximilian of Habsburg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And through that marriage the Burgundian lands, Luxembourg included, passed to the Habsburg family.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That was the beginning of an era in which Luxembourg belonged to the most powerful dynasty in the world.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Maximilian and Mary's grandson was born in Ghent in the year 1500 and grew up to be Charles the Fifth, who ruled Spain, much of Italy, the Netherlands, Germany, and the new Spanish lands in the Americas.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Luxembourg was a tiny corner of all that.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But it sat right on the road between his Netherlands and his Italian and Spanish possessions, so it mattered.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What happened when Charles retired?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His empire was divided. His son Philip the Second took Spain and the Netherlands, and Luxembourg went with them.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That put Luxembourg in the front row for one of the great conflicts of the age.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The northern provinces of the Netherlands rose in revolt, turned Protestant, and eventually broke away to become the Dutch Republic.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But not the south.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The southern provinces, including Luxembourg, stayed under Spain and stayed Catholic.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Luxembourg's people had barely been touched by the Reformation, and they remained loyal.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the seventeenth century was brutal.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: During the Thirty Years' War, armies marched back and forth across the Luxembourg countryside, looting and burning.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Famine and plague followed the soldiers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In some parts of the country, the population fell by something like half.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Meanwhile Spain was declining, and France under the Sun King, Louis the Fourteenth, was rising.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And France began nibbling.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1659, the peace treaty between Spain and France handed over a belt of towns along Luxembourg's southern border, including Thionville.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was the first of several times that Luxembourg would shrink.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Then Louis came for the fortress itself.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1684. French forces besieged the city for about a month and took it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And here the history of the place changes.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Louis brought the great military engineer Marquis de Vauban, the greatest builder of fortresses of his age, to rebuild the defenses.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What did Vauban do?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He dug ditches, raised massive walls, and tunneled deep into the rock.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Within a few years, the capital of Luxembourg was one of the most formidable fortresses in Europe, with a nickname that would stick: the Gibraltar of the North.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the French didn't keep it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1697, after a long war, Louis gave Luxembourg back to Spain in the Treaty of Ryswick.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: France held it again briefly in the early eighteenth century, and when the great war over the Spanish throne was settled in 1713 and 1714, Luxembourg was handed to the Austrian branch of the Habsburgs, together with what is now Belgium.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Those lands became the Austrian Netherlands, and Luxembourg was a part of them.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How was the Austrian period?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: About eight decades, sometimes remembered as a relatively calm and prosperous time.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Historians still debate whether it was really a golden age, but the evidence of peace is clear enough.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The population recovered. Ironworks along the rivers produced cast iron, and farming improved.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the fortress got bigger.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Austrians kept strengthening it, and in the seventeen-thirties they built a new fort on the plateau across the valley, called Fort Thüngen.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Its restored towers, nicknamed the Three Acorns, still stand today, and now they house a museum.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the real wonder is hidden.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Over the generations, engineers dug a vast network of tunnels, called casemates, into the sandstone cliff of the Bock.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They provided shelter for soldiers, space for cannon, and storage for supplies.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At the height of the fortress, there were many miles of tunnels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Today, roughly seventeen kilometers of them survive, about ten and a half miles, and visitors can still walk through them and look out over the valley through the gun slits.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The fortress changed hands so often.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Its history reads like a revolving door.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: If you were an ambitious king, Luxembourg was a prize.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: If you lived in Luxembourg, it was a burden.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The city was stuffed with soldiers, the townspeople paid for the upkeep of the walls, and every time a war broke out between France and its neighbors, armies tramped across your fields.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the quiet ended in the seventeen-eighties.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Emperor Joseph the Second, who ruled from Vienna, was a reformer of the enlightened kind.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He tried to modernize his lands all at once, closing monasteries, limiting the church's power, and reorganizing the courts.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Many of his subjects in the Austrian Netherlands, including Luxembourg, were conservative and devout, and they were furious.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1789, the same year the French Revolution began, a revolt broke out in the Netherlands.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was suppressed within a couple of years.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the French Revolution wasn't so easily suppressed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1794, French revolutionary armies swept through the Austrian Netherlands.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Luxembourg fortress held out.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For about seven months, from the autumn of 1794, French troops surrounded it while Austrian defenders waited for relief that never came.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And it fell.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In June 1795, starving and cut off, the garrison surrendered.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Gibraltar of the North had fallen, and not to a great assault but to hunger.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What happened to the duchy?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the autumn of 1795, France formally annexed the territory.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The old duchy of Luxembourg ceased to exist, and in its place the French created a new administrative unit called the Department of the Forests, named for the heavily wooded Ardennes hills.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was ruled from the city of Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the French years brought change.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Profound change. The old feudal rights were abolished.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The church lost much of its land.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A new system of laws, the Napoleonic Code, was introduced, and traces of it survive in Luxembourg's legal system to this day.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But there was a price.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A heavy one. The French demanded soldiers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Young men from Luxembourg were drafted into Napoleon's armies, and many never came home.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1798, the conscription law sparked a revolt in the countryside of the north.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Peasants armed with clubs, farm tools, and old hunting guns rose up against the French.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The Peasants' War.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Or more literally, the War of the Clubs.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was crushed within weeks, and the leaders were punished harshly.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But the memory of it has never faded.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For generations, it was a powerful reminder of how deeply the ordinary people of Luxembourg resented foreign rule.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then 1814.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: After Napoleon's disastrous retreat from Russia and his defeat at Leipzig, the French withdrew.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For the first time in centuries, the future of Luxembourg was up for negotiation among the great powers of Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: In the next chapter, they make a decision that creates something no one had ever seen before.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A grand duchy.
